items.title: Level 5: Choosing the strongest STAR answer
items.body: When two answers describe the same event, the stronger one is usually the one that shows the Behaviour through specific actions, in the first person, with a measurable result. Consider the question 'Give an example of when you delivered work to a deadline.' Answer one: 'I volunteer at a food bank and we get very busy. I always make sure the work is done on time because I am reliable. We usually finish by closing.' Answer two: 'At the food bank, forty parcels had to be packed before the van left at 2 pm, and I was running the packing table. I listed the items for each parcel, put the heaviest in first, asked two helpers to switch to checking labels at 1.15 and packed twenty myself. All forty were loaded by 1.55. I learned to ask for helpers earlier.' Answer two wins because it has a time, a number, a clear responsibility, ordered actions and a result with a lesson. Answer one describes a habit, uses 'we' and offers a claim of being reliable. An answer can also fail by being too narrow. If the question is about delivering at pace and the writer only describes accuracy, the assessor cannot give marks for the Behaviour asked. Similarly, an answer can fail by being about someone else's decision. When choosing between answers in practice, ask which one lets the assessor picture what you did, which one matches the Behaviour in the question, and which one would survive a follow-up question.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes Answer two stronger than Answer one in the food bank example?

options.text: It is longer and uses more formal vocabulary throughout
It states that the writer is reliable and works hard each day
It describes the usual busy periods at the food bank in detail
A time, a number, ordered actions and a result with a lesson

questions.hint: Specific, ordered actions and a measurable result make evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I always make sure the work is done on time because I am reliable' weak evidence?

options.text: It does not use enough numbers to be taken seriously
It is too specific to be believed by an assessor
It is a claim about character, not a described action
It is written in the wrong tense for an application

questions.hint: Claims about yourself do not show what you did.

questions.prompt: An applicant answers a question on delivering at pace by describing only how carefully she checked each form. What is the main problem?

options.text: The answer contains no Situation to explain the background
The answer shows accuracy, not the Behaviour asked for
The answer is too short to be counted as a STAR example
The answer is too honest about how long the checking took

questions.hint: The answer must match the Behaviour in the question.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good test of an answer's strength?

options.text: Whether it uses we
Whether it contains the longest words
Whether it mentions an employer
Whether it would survive follow-up questions

questions.hint: If the story is real and specific it stands up to questioning.

questions.prompt: In Answer two, what does asking two helpers to switch to checking labels show?

options.text: Avoidance of responsibility by passing jobs to others
Poor planning at the start of the packing session
Reorganising work to meet a deadline
A wish to hand the whole job over to the helpers

questions.hint: It is an action taken to protect the deadline.

questions.prompt: Which sentence from Answer two is the Result?

options.text: I was running the packing table.
I listed the items for each parcel.
All forty were loaded by 1.55.
Forty parcels had to be packed before 2 pm.

questions.hint: It states the outcome, with a time.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes a team decision made by her manager and says 'we decided'. Why will she probably score badly?

options.text: She named her manager, which is not allowed in an answer
She used a number that the panel cannot easily check
The assessor cannot see what she personally did
She mentioned a deadline, which weakens the answer

questions.hint: The answer must be about her own actions.

questions.prompt: Which change would most improve 'I volunteer at a food bank and we get very busy'?

options.text: Add the names of all the other helpers who work with her
Add a specific occasion, her responsibility, steps and result
Add the opening hours of the food bank and the days it is open
Add a sentence about how much she enjoys helping local people

questions.hint: A specific occasion with steps and a result makes a STAR answer.

questions.prompt: Which question does the passage suggest asking to choose between two answers?

options.text: Which one is the longest of the two answers?
Which lets the assessor picture what you did?
Which uses the most adjectives to describe the writer?
Which mentions the most people who were involved?

questions.hint: Picturing the actions is the main test.

questions.prompt: What lesson does Answer two end with?

options.text: Pack heavier items last
Work more slowly
Ask for helpers earlier
Avoid busy periods

questions.hint: It gives a reflection that is useful for next time.

items.title: Level 5: Matching a situation to the best Behaviour
items.body: In an assessment or application you may need to decide which Behaviour a situation best shows, and then build your answer around it. Here are some worked cases. Case one: a woman is asked to hand over a task to a new colleague. She writes a one-page guide with screenshots, sits with the colleague for an hour, and asks him to try it alone while she watches. This is mainly Developing Self and Others, because she helped another person learn. It also shows Communicating, but the main purpose was development. Case two: a man notices that three customers a week ring to ask for the same document. He drafts a short information sheet, gets his supervisor's approval and starts sending it with the original letter. This is mainly Changing and Improving because he acted on a problem to prevent it. Case three: a volunteer is told the hall is double-booked on the morning of an event. She phones both groups, checks the other available rooms, calls the one with the closest start time and agrees a swap. This is mainly Making Effective Decisions, with some Communicating. Case four: a school secretary realises that a late reply to a parent could mean a child misses a trip, so she answers the message within the hour. This is Seeing the Big Picture. Notice that each case turns on the purpose of the action. Ask what the person was trying to achieve and which Behaviour's definition matches.

questions.prompt: A woman writes a guide, sits with a new colleague and watches him try the task alone. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Delivering at Pace
Leadership
Developing Self and Others

questions.hint: Her purpose was to help another person learn.

questions.prompt: A man drafts an information sheet because three customers a week ask for the same document. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Changing and Improving
Managing a Quality Service
Seeing the Big Picture
Working Together

questions.hint: He acted on a recurring problem to prevent it.

questions.prompt: A volunteer learns the hall is double-booked, checks rooms, and agrees a swap with one group. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Developing Self and Others
Delivering at Pace
Making Effective Decisions
Changing and Improving

questions.hint: She weighed options and chose a workable solution.

questions.prompt: A secretary replies within the hour because a late answer could mean a child misses a trip. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Making Effective Decisions
Communicating and Influencing
Managing a Quality Service
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: She linked her task to the effect on a child and family.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to decide which Behaviour a situation shows?

options.text: Ask what the person was trying to achieve
Count the number of people involved
Check where it happened
Look at the length of the story

questions.hint: The purpose of the action points to the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: In the double-booked hall case, which Behaviour supports the main one?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service, as she kept a record
Developing Self and Others, as she learned from the problem
Communicating and Influencing, as she phoned both groups
Leadership, as she managed the volunteers

questions.hint: Phoning the groups and agreeing a swap involves communicating.

questions.prompt: In the handover case, why is Developing Self and Others better than Communicating?

options.text: Communicating is not an entry-level Behaviour
The main purpose was to help the colleague learn
The guide was written, not spoken
The colleague asked questions

questions.hint: The purpose decides the main Behaviour.

questions.prompt: A man's information sheet needed his supervisor's approval. What does this show?

options.text: He ignored the procedures of the office to get his own way
He avoided taking responsibility by passing the decision upwards
He lacked confidence in his own idea and needed approval for it
He worked within the proper process while improving things

questions.hint: Seeking approval fits with Managing a Quality Service and sensible change.

questions.prompt: A helper notices a rota gap, texts three people and finds a cover by evening. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Working Together
Changing and Improving
Developing Self and Others

questions.hint: She acted to make the group's plan work with others' help.

questions.prompt: A person ranks eight tasks, finishes the three urgent ones by noon and tells her manager the rest will follow. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Making Effective Decisions
Delivering at Pace
Developing Self and Others
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: Prioritising and communicating progress against time is Delivering at Pace.

items.title: Level 5: Planning from a real AO advert
items.body: Suppose you read an advert for an Administrative Officer that says candidates will be assessed on Behaviours (Communicating and Influencing, Managing a Quality Service), Strengths and Ability. The application form asks for a personal statement of 500 words covering the two Behaviours, and the later stages include an online test and an interview. A sensible plan has several steps. Step one: pick a different story for each Behaviour from your bank. For Communicating and Influencing, you might choose helping a neighbour with a benefit letter. For Managing a Quality Service, you might choose keeping accurate attendance records at a youth club. Step two: write each as about 200 words in STAR form, leaving a margin for the word limit. Step three: practise sample tests, ideally in the same conditions as the real test. Step four: reflect on your strengths by listing things you enjoy and why, so that you can speak naturally at interview. Step five: look at the date of every stage and put them in a diary. If you need an adjustment for the test or the interview, ask early. Step six: keep copies of everything you submit. Notice what you do not do. You do not prepare for Technical, because none is listed. You do not write about all nine Behaviours. You do not copy a general answer from another source. A tight plan based on the advert gets the most from your time.

questions.prompt: How many words should each story be if the statement is 500 words covering two Behaviours?

options.text: About 200 each, leaving a margin
About 1,000 each, with the extra words trimmed afterwards
About 500 each, which the form will cut down automatically
About 50 each, so that the statement is brief and neat

questions.hint: Two stories of about 200 words leave room for a margin.

questions.prompt: Which story suits Managing a Quality Service best?

options.text: Helping a neighbour with a benefit letter
Suggesting a new colour for a poster
Welcoming a nervous new volunteer
Keeping accurate attendance records at a youth club

questions.hint: Accurate records show quality.

questions.prompt: Which story suits Communicating and Influencing best?

options.text: Learning to use a new database at a local charity
Helping a neighbour understand a benefit letter
Packing parcels at a food bank before the van arrives
Keeping an accurate register for a youth club each week

questions.hint: Explaining clearly to someone who needs it fits communicating.

questions.prompt: Which step helps you speak naturally in the Strengths stage?

options.text: Learning a script
Practising Numerical tests
Listing things you enjoy and why
Writing a STAR for each strength

questions.hint: Knowing what you enjoy lets you answer honestly.

questions.prompt: Why practise sample tests in the same conditions as the real one?

options.text: So that you can memorise the answers to the real questions
So that you can skip the instructions on the day
So you know the layout and pace and avoid surprises
So that the real test will be shorter than the practice

questions.hint: Familiar conditions reduce stress and improve pacing.

questions.prompt: Which of these should this applicant NOT spend time on?

options.text: Choosing the stories she will use for the two Behaviours
Practising sample tests before the online test opens
A Technical qualification, because none is listed
The dates and times of each stage of the recruitment

questions.hint: Only the elements listed in the advert need preparation.

questions.prompt: Why put every stage date in a diary?

options.text: So that the dates cannot be changed by the recruiter
So that you can reschedule the stages as often as you like
So that you do not miss a deadline or interview
So that the panel can look at the diary at the interview

questions.hint: Missing a date can end an application.

questions.prompt: When should the applicant ask for a test or interview adjustment?

options.text: On the day
After the results
At the final stage only
As early as possible

questions.hint: Early requests give time to arrange it.

questions.prompt: Why keep copies of everything you submit?

options.text: So you can send them to other jobs unchanged
Because the Civil Service asks for them back
So you can edit them after the deadline
So you can recall what you said before the interview

questions.hint: You may be asked about your answers later.

questions.prompt: Which action would waste the applicant's limited time?

options.text: Writing about all nine Behaviours
Planning the dates of each stage in a diary
Practising sample tests at home before the real one
Choosing two stories from her bank of examples

questions.hint: Only the listed Behaviours are assessed.

items.title: Level 5: Improving a draft: which edit helps most?
items.body: When you review your own answer, you often find several faults at once. The skill is to decide which single edit would improve it the most. Here is a draft for Working Together: 'We had a big job at the community centre. Everyone worked together and it was great. I enjoy being part of a team. The manager was pleased.' The faults are many. There is no Task, no named actions, no numbers, 'we' hides the writer, and the Result has no measure. Which edit helps most? The strongest single edit is to add what the writer personally did, for example 'I agreed with two other helpers that I would set up the tables while they cooked, then I carried the chairs and swapped with Mina when her shift ended'. This fills the Action, which carries the most marks and which currently has nothing. Adding a number to the Result would help, but a number alone would still leave the assessor with nothing to score for the Behaviour. Changing the opening sentence would help only a little. Removing the sentence about enjoying teams helps, since it is a claim, but it does not add evidence. After the Action is repaired, the next edits are to add a Task and a measurable Result. A useful rule when time is short is to repair in this order: Action first, then Result, then Task, then Situation. Fix pronouns as you go, because they are quick to change.

questions.prompt: Which single edit would improve the Working Together draft most?

options.text: Changing the opening sentence so that it sounds more lively
Adding a longer Situation to explain the community centre
Adding what the writer personally did, step by step
Removing the last sentence, which mentions the manager

questions.hint: The Action carries the most marks and is empty.

questions.prompt: Why does adding a number to the Result help less than adding an Action?

options.text: The assessor ignores numbers in short application answers
A number alone leaves nothing to score for the Behaviour
Numbers are not allowed in the Result part of an answer
Numbers make the answer too long to fit within the word limit

questions.hint: The Behaviour is shown by actions.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with 'I enjoy being part of a team'?

options.text: It is too specific for an application at this level
It is written in the past tense, which is not allowed
It is a rude thing to say about the other members
It is a claim that adds no evidence

questions.hint: Claims do not show what you did.

questions.prompt: In what order does the passage suggest repairing a draft when time is short?

options.text: Task, Situation, Result, Action
Situation, Task, Action, Result
Result, Situation, Task, Action
Action, Result, Task, Situation

questions.hint: The Action carries the most marks, so it comes first.

questions.prompt: Which of these is missing from the Working Together draft altogether?

options.text: A Situation
The word we
A mention of the manager
A Task

questions.hint: It never says what the writer was responsible for.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would be the best Action?

options.text: It was a big job and the whole group did well to finish it
The manager thanked all of the helpers at the end of the day
I set up the tables while two helpers cooked, then carried chairs
Everyone helped out where they could to get the lunch ready on time

questions.hint: It lists specific steps that show cooperation.

questions.prompt: Why change 'we' to 'I' as you go?

options.text: It adds a number to the answer without extra work
It removes the need for a Situation in the answer
It is quick and shows your own part
It makes the answer shorter in nearly every case

questions.hint: It is a quick fix with large effect.

questions.prompt: The sentence 'The manager was pleased' is what in STAR terms?

options.text: A Situation that sets the scene for the reader
A weak Result with no measure
A Task that explains what the writer was asked to do
An Action that shows what the writer did herself

questions.hint: It reports a reaction but not a measure or lesson.

questions.prompt: Which edit would improve the Result most after the Action is repaired?

options.text: Making it longer
Adding more adjectives
Moving it to the start
Adding a measure and a lesson

questions.hint: A measurable outcome and a lesson make a strong Result.

questions.prompt: Why is changing the opening sentence a low priority?

options.text: It is always correct
It adds little evidence of the Behaviour
It breaks the word limit
It is the only sentence the assessor reads

questions.hint: Evidence of the Behaviour is in the Action.

items.title: Level 5: Handling follow-up questions at interview
items.body: After you give an example, interviewers often ask follow-up questions to test depth and honesty. They are not trying to trip you up. They want to see that the story is yours. Common follow-ups include 'What was your role compared with the others?', 'What would you have done if that had not worked?', 'How did you feel about it at the time?', 'What would you do differently now?' and 'Can you give me an exact figure?' Strong candidates prepare short, honest answers. For a question about the role of others, they name what others did without taking credit. For 'what if it had not worked', they describe a back-up they considered, even if they did not need it. For 'what would you do differently', they give a real lesson and not a false one such as 'I would work even harder'. For 'exact figure', they say 'about' if they are unsure. A candidate who cannot answer may feel panicked, but there are sensible options. Take a breath. Say 'Let me think for a moment.' If you truly do not remember, say so and give what you do remember. Do not invent. If the panel moves on to a different example, treat it as a fresh start. Try not to dwell on one weak answer, since each question is scored separately. After the interview, note down any follow-ups you found hard, and use them to improve your stories.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks 'What was your role compared with the others?' Which answer is best?

options.text: I set up the tables, and two other helpers cooked and served
It was a team effort and we all did everything together
I did most of it myself and the others helped me a bit
I cannot remember who did which part of the work

questions.hint: A clear split of roles without taking credit for others' work.

questions.prompt: Asked 'What would you do differently?', which is the most useful answer?

options.text: I would avoid taking on that kind of task again
I would ask for extra helpers earlier, since we ran short at noon
I would work even harder next time and try not to stop
I would do nothing differently, as it all went perfectly

questions.hint: A real, specific lesson shows reflection.

questions.prompt: Asked 'Can you give me an exact figure?' when unsure, what should you say?

options.text: About £300, but I'm not certain of the exact sum
I never count money, so it was not something I recorded
The figure does not matter, as the result was good anyway
Exactly £300, because it is better to sound sure of yourself

questions.hint: Approximation is honest.

questions.prompt: Asked 'What if that had not worked?', which answer is strongest?

options.text: It had to work, so I did not consider anything else
The manager would have decided
I would have given up
I had thought of asking another group to share the load

questions.hint: Describing a back-up plan shows judgement.

questions.prompt: What can you say if you need a moment to think?

options.text: Skip that question
Next question please
Let me think for a moment
I don't know

questions.hint: A short pause is acceptable and looks better than rushing.

questions.prompt: If you truly do not remember a detail, what should you do?

options.text: Invent a detail that fits the rest of the story
Say that the event did not happen at all
Say so and give what you do remember
Change the subject to something you do remember

questions.hint: Honesty is better than invention.

questions.prompt: What should you do after a weak answer to one question?

options.text: Ask the panel to repeat the earlier question twice
Give up on the interview
Treat the next question as a fresh start
Apologise at length

questions.hint: Each question is scored separately.

questions.prompt: Why do interviewers ask follow-up questions?

options.text: To use up the time left at the end of the interview
To trip you up when you have given a good answer
To check the story is yours and has depth
To change the topic when they have heard enough

questions.hint: Their purpose is to test depth and honesty.

questions.prompt: How can you improve your stories after an interview?

options.text: Avoid applying for similar interviews in the near future
Memorise the panel's questions so you can repeat the answers
Delete the stories that were not asked about on the day
Note down follow-ups that were hard and prepare for them

questions.hint: Reflection leads to better preparation.

questions.prompt: Which follow-up answer shows credit-taking?

options.text: Two others did the cooking
I arranged the rota with Mina
I did the tables and Mina did the serving
I did most of it myself

questions.hint: It overclaims when others contributed.

items.title: Level 5: Using career breaks and caring in an application
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many applicants have gaps in their paid work because they were caring for children, looking after a relative, dealing with illness or moving country. A gap does not need an apology, but it does need an honest, brief and positive explanation, and the skills you used during it can count as Experience. Take a person who left work for five years to care for her father. She could write: 'From 2019 to 2024 I was the main carer for my father, who had dementia. I managed his medication and appointments, dealt with the council and the bank on his behalf, kept his accounts, and worked with three care agencies to arrange cover.' This shows planning, communicating, accuracy and working with others. She could use the same experience for Managing a Quality Service by describing how she kept a medication log, for Communicating and Influencing by describing a meeting with social services, and for Delivering at Pace by explaining how she handled several appointments a week. She should not claim to have run a business or managed staff, if she did not. She should give dates and the main responsibilities, and say what she learned. If the form asks about gaps, she answers directly in a sentence or two and moves on to what she can offer. If she has been out of work for a long time, a short course or volunteering can help refresh her confidence and give recent examples, though it is not required.

questions.prompt: How should a career gap spent caring be described?

options.text: By hiding the dates so that the gap is not noticed
With a long apology that explains why you were away from work
Honestly and briefly, then move to the skills used
With no explanation, in the hope that nobody asks about it

questions.hint: A brief honest explanation followed by skills works best.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best describes caring experience in work language?

options.text: I stayed at home with my father because he needed some company
I managed my father's medication and appointments and dealt with the council for him
I just looked after my dad for a while when he was not very well
I did what I could for him, which was not really proper work

questions.hint: It gives actions and responsibilities with dates.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour could a medication log best support?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Leadership
Changing and Improving
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: Accurate records show quality.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour could a meeting with social services best support?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing
Delivering at Pace
Developing Self and Others
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: Speaking for someone to an organisation is communicating and influencing.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour could handling several appointments a week best support?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Delivering at Pace
Making Effective Decisions
Leadership

questions.hint: Planning around fixed times is Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: What should the carer NOT claim?

options.text: That she managed her father's medication and appointments
That she ran a business or managed staff, if she did not
That she kept his accounts and dealt with the bank for him
That she worked with three care agencies to arrange cover

questions.hint: False claims will fail under follow-up.

questions.prompt: If the form asks about a gap, how should she answer?

options.text: Directly in a sentence or two, then move to what she can offer
With a long and detailed account of her father's illness
By describing a short job that she did not actually hold
By leaving the answer blank so that the panel asks at interview

questions.hint: A short, direct answer is enough.

questions.prompt: What can help someone out of work for a long time refresh their confidence?

options.text: A new job title
A short course or volunteering
A letter from a friend
Waiting a year

questions.hint: Recent activity gives new examples, though it is not required.

questions.prompt: Which element does caring for a relative most directly support?

options.text: Technical
Ability
Strengths
Experience

questions.hint: It shows what she has done and learned.

questions.prompt: What should she include to make the account strong?

options.text: Dates, main responsibilities and what she learned
The father's detailed medical history and his diagnosis
An apology for the gap in her paid work history
A list of her feelings about being a carer for so many years

questions.hint: Dates, duties and learning make it evidence.

items.title: Level 5: Strengths questions in situations
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths questions are quick, so it helps to think through how you would answer a few typical ones. Take 'What do you enjoy most about your day?' A natural answer might be 'I like the moment when a task I have been sorting out comes together, such as when I have tidied a messy spreadsheet and everything adds up. It gives me a lift.' This shows energy and a link to administrative work. Compare it with an answer that is false: 'I love every minute of work.' That is not believable. Next, 'Would you rather work on one task at a time or several?' A good answer is honest: 'I prefer to finish one thing before starting another, but I can switch when the phones are busy.' It shows a preference and flexibility. 'What do you find hard?' deserves an honest, brief answer that shows you manage it: 'I find it hard to leave a job unfinished at the end of the day, so I make a short list for the morning.' An answer that claims no weakness may sound unrealistic. 'What are you good at that people do not see?' might bring: 'I notice small errors, and I always check names.' These answers are short and use no STAR structure. They are given at speed, so do not rehearse long scripts. Instead, know your preferences, be honest, and add a brief reason.

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'What do you enjoy most about your day?' sounds most natural?

options.text: I like the moment when a messy spreadsheet finally adds up
I love every single minute of my working day without exception
I do not mind either way, as long as the day goes by quickly
I enjoy the end of the day most, when I can go home and relax

questions.hint: It is specific and shows genuine energy.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I love every minute of work' a weak strengths answer?

options.text: It is too long
It uses a number
It is not believable
It is too specific

questions.hint: Panels listen for honest, credible answers.

questions.prompt: Which answer is best to 'one task at a time or several?'

options.text: I prefer to finish one thing first, but can switch when the phones are busy
I can only ever work on one thing and will not switch for anyone
I do not mind either way and have no preference at all
I can do twenty things at the same time and never make a mistake

questions.hint: It is honest and shows flexibility.

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'What do you find hard?' is most useful?

options.text: I find most of the work hard, but I try to get through each day
I honestly find nothing hard, because I always manage to cope well
I would rather not say, as it is not something I think about
I find it hard to leave a job unfinished, so I make a list for the morning

questions.hint: It is honest and shows how you manage it.

questions.prompt: Why might a claim of having no weaknesses sound unrealistic?

options.text: Everyone has things they find hard
It is too long to be believed by a panel
It is written in the past tense by mistake
It uses too many numbers for a short answer

questions.hint: Honest answers are more credible.

questions.prompt: Which strength fits an administrative role?

options.text: Making sales calls
Enjoying loud, crowded places
Lifting heavy loads
Noticing small errors and checking names

questions.hint: It links to accuracy in admin work.

questions.prompt: Should a strengths answer use the STAR structure?

options.text: It should follow STAR in full
It should be written out first
It should be short and natural, without STAR
It should be over two minutes long

questions.hint: Strengths questions are quick and natural.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to prepare for strengths questions?

options.text: Learn long scripts and say them in the order they were written
Write a full STAR story for each of the things you enjoy
Ask the panel at the start what they would like to hear
Know your preferences, be honest and add a brief reason

questions.hint: Knowing yourself is the best preparation.

questions.prompt: What does a brief reason add to a strengths answer?

options.text: It replaces the answer
It shows why you feel that way
It changes the topic
It makes the answer longer

questions.hint: A reason makes the answer more convincing.

questions.prompt: A panel hears 'I am a perfectionist' as a weakness answer. What risk is there?

options.text: It can sound like a rehearsed line rather than an honest answer
It is too short to be scored by the panel as a proper answer
It is not allowed under the rules for strengths-based interviews
It is always seen as the ideal answer to give about a weakness

questions.hint: Stock phrases can sound insincere.

items.title: Level 5: Judgement and numerical situations
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Practice for the Ability stage is easier when you see how typical questions work. In a judgement test you might read: 'You notice a colleague has made an error in a form that is due to go out today. She is on leave. What would you do?' The options might be to ignore it, to correct it yourself without telling anyone, to tell your manager and agree how to put it right, or to send the form as it is. The best response is the third, because it fixes the error openly and follows the proper process. It reflects honesty, integrity and sound judgement. The worst might be to ignore the error. A numerical question might give a table: 'Letters received: Monday 120, Tuesday 90, Wednesday 105, Thursday 85, Friday 100. What is the average per day?' The total is 500, and 500 divided by 5 is 100. Another might say: 'A team handled 240 calls on Monday and 20% fewer on Tuesday. How many calls on Tuesday?' Twenty per cent of 240 is 48, so Tuesday was 192. In a verbal test you may read: 'All staff must sign in by 9 am. Late arrivals must report to reception.' The statement 'Staff who arrive at 9.30 must report to reception' is true from the passage, because 9.30 is after 9 am. The statement 'Reception opens at 8.30' cannot be said, because the passage does not mention it. Always answer from the information given.

questions.prompt: A colleague on leave has made an error in a form due out today. What is the best response in a judgement test?

options.text: Wait until she returns from leave before doing anything
Ignore it and send the form as it stands
Correct it secretly and say nothing to anybody
Tell your manager and agree how to put it right

questions.hint: It fixes the error openly and follows the process.

questions.prompt: Which response in the same situation is the worst?

options.text: Ignoring the error and sending the form as it is
Asking another colleague whether she knows how to fix it
Checking the office guidance on correcting forms before sending
Telling the manager about the error and asking what to do

questions.hint: Ignoring a known error is the least responsible choice.

questions.prompt: Letters received were 120, 90, 105, 85 and 100. What is the average per day?
questions.hint: The total is 500, and 500 divided by 5 is 100.

questions.prompt: A team handled 240 calls on Monday and 20% fewer on Tuesday. How many calls on Tuesday?
questions.hint: 20% of 240 is 48, and 240 minus 48 is 192.

questions.prompt: Passage: All staff must sign in by 9 am. Late arrivals must report to reception. Is 'Staff who arrive at 9.30 must report to reception' true, false or cannot say?

options.text: True
False
It depends on the day
Cannot say

questions.hint: 9.30 is after 9 am, so the passage supports it.

questions.prompt: From the same passage, what is 'Reception opens at 8.30'?

options.text: False, since late arrivals report there after the 9 am sign-in
Cannot say, as the passage gives no opening time
True on weekdays only, as staff sign in on those days
True, since staff must sign in by 9 am and reception handles it

questions.hint: The passage gives no opening time.

questions.prompt: Which values does the best judgement answer reflect?

options.text: Loyalty to one colleague above the needs of the work
Honesty, integrity and sound judgement
Avoiding all conflict, whatever the cost to the customer
Speed, secrecy and keeping things to yourself

questions.hint: These match the Civil Service values.

questions.prompt: What should you use to answer a verbal reasoning statement?

options.text: Only the information in the passage
What most people think
What the examiner says
Your own general knowledge

questions.hint: The passage is the only source.

questions.prompt: A table shows 40, 55, 35, 50 and 60 enquiries. What is the difference between the highest and lowest day?
questions.hint: 60 minus 35 is 25.

questions.prompt: Why is secretly correcting a colleague's error a weaker answer than telling the manager?

options.text: It is less open and does not follow the proper process
It takes much longer than speaking to the manager does
It is of no help to the colleague or to the customer
It is dishonest towards the manager but not towards anyone else

questions.hint: Openness and process matter in these tests.

items.title: Level 5: Honesty dilemmas when applying
items.body: Honesty can be tested by small decisions as you prepare. Take a person who wants to use an example from a job she held for only two weeks. She could say 'I worked there for two weeks' or she could leave out the dates and let the assessor assume it was a long time. The honest and still effective option is to give the dates and focus on what she did in that time. Another case: a man led a team on a project at college, but another student actually did most of the planning. He should say what he personally did, such as chairing meetings and writing the final report, and not take credit for the plan. A third case: a candidate is not sure if a charity role counts as experience of working with the public. She should describe the role honestly, with dates and duties, and let the assessor decide. A fourth case: a candidate who forgot the date of a test deadline finds she cannot submit. She should contact the recruiter, explain honestly and ask, without pretending to have had a technical problem. A fifth case: a person is asked at interview whether she has any criminal convictions to declare, and she has one that is spent. The rules about spent convictions are specific, so she should read the guidance on the advert and ask if unsure, and not guess. In every case the rule is the same: say what is true, say it clearly, and let the assessor judge.

questions.prompt: A job lasted only two weeks. What is the honest and still effective approach?

options.text: Say that it lasted several months to give the example weight
Give the dates and focus on what she did in that time
Avoid mentioning the job and use a different example instead
Leave out the dates and let the reader assume it was longer

questions.hint: Being open about dates keeps the account honest.

questions.prompt: A student led a project but another did most of the planning. What should he say?

options.text: That the whole team did everything and he took no particular part
That he did all of the planning himself, since he led the project
Nothing about the plan, and describe only the final presentation
What he did himself, such as chairing meetings and writing the report

questions.hint: He should claim only his own part.

questions.prompt: A candidate is unsure if a charity role counts as working with the public. What should she do?

options.text: Leave it out, since only paid roles count as working with the public
Describe it honestly with dates and duties and let the assessor decide
Claim that it counts without giving the dates or the duties
Ask the panel at interview to say whether it counts or not

questions.hint: Honest description lets the assessor judge.

questions.prompt: A candidate missed a test deadline. What is the best action?

options.text: Contact the recruiter, explain honestly and ask
Give up
Submit late without comment
Pretend to have had a technical problem

questions.hint: Honest explanation is the right approach.

questions.prompt: A candidate has a spent conviction and is asked about convictions. What should she do?

options.text: Guess the answer that seems safest to her
Read the guidance on the advert and ask if unsure
Ignore the question and move on to the next one
Say that she has none without checking the guidance

questions.hint: The rules are specific, so check them.

questions.prompt: What is the rule common to every case?

options.text: Say what you think the panel would most like to hear
Say as little as possible so that nothing can be checked later
Say what is true, say it clearly and let the assessor judge
Say whatever sounds best for the job on offer in the advert

questions.hint: This is the honest approach.

questions.prompt: What might happen if the assessor assumed a two-week job was long?

options.text: The story could fall apart under follow-up questions
Nothing would happen, since assessors do not ask about dates
The score would rise, as longer jobs are always given more marks
The panel would not notice, because dates are never checked

questions.hint: Misleading omissions can be exposed.

questions.prompt: What shows integrity when a team result is shared?

options.text: Refusing to talk about it
Taking all credit
Saying nothing about the team
Naming what others contributed

questions.hint: Giving others credit is honest.

questions.prompt: Which action is dishonest?

options.text: Pretending to have had a technical problem
Reading the guidance on the advert more than once
Admitting that a deadline was missed by mistake
Asking the recruiter whether a late entry is possible

questions.hint: It is a false excuse.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to guess about spent convictions?

options.text: It is always safe to say you have none, whatever the guidance says
The panel never asks about convictions at this level of job
It is a trick question that the panel uses to test applicants
The rules are specific, and a wrong guess can cause problems later

questions.hint: Check the guidance rather than guess.

items.title: Level 5: Making the most of a limited word count
items.body: Application forms often limit each answer to a set number of words or characters, and the limit can feel tight. The best approach is to write the full STAR answer first, aim for a little under the limit, and then check that each part is doing a job. A rough guide for a 250-word answer is about 30 words on the Situation and Task together, 140 on the Action, and 60 on the Result, with the rest as margin. Cut descriptive detail that is not needed, such as the history of the group, and long introductions. Keep numbers, because they pack a lot of evidence into few words. Replace long phrases with shorter ones: 'in order to' becomes 'to', and 'at that point in time' becomes 'then'. Use active verbs, which are shorter than passive ones. Remove repeated information. Do not remove the Result to save space, since a story without an outcome loses marks. Do not squash the answer into one block of text, since it is harder to read, though some forms do not allow paragraphs. If the form counts characters, check how it counts spaces. Read the answer aloud after cutting to be sure it still makes sense. Finally, paste it into the form only when you are happy, and save a copy. Some online forms time out, so it is wise to type answers elsewhere first.

questions.prompt: For a 250-word answer, roughly how many words suit the Action?

options.text: About 10
About 140
About 20
About 200

questions.hint: The Action should take the largest share.

questions.prompt: What should you cut first to save words?

options.text: The numbers that show the size and scale of what you did
The active verbs that describe the steps you took
The Result at the end, as the assessor can usually infer it
Background detail such as a group's history

questions.hint: Descriptive detail adds little evidence.

questions.prompt: Which change saves words without losing meaning?

options.text: Removing all the numbers from the answer
Using longer words in place of the shorter ones
Replacing 'in order to' with 'to'
Removing the Action to leave space for the Result

questions.hint: Shorter phrasing keeps the meaning.

questions.prompt: Why keep numbers when cutting?

options.text: They add length to an answer that is too short
They pack a lot of evidence into few words
They are required by the application form for each answer
They make the answer look more decorative and neat

questions.hint: Numbers are efficient evidence.

questions.prompt: Why not remove the Result to save space?

options.text: The Result is the longest part
A story with no outcome loses marks
The Result is unimportant
The form requires it be last

questions.hint: The Result gives the evidence of effect.

questions.prompt: Why type answers elsewhere before pasting them into an online form?

options.text: The form cannot accept text typed straight into the boxes
The assessor prefers answers that have been pasted in
Some forms time out and you could lose your work
Typing elsewhere automatically makes the answer shorter

questions.hint: A saved copy protects your work.

questions.prompt: What should you do after cutting an answer?

options.text: Add more adjectives so that it sounds more impressive
Send it off without reading it again, to save time
Read it aloud to check it still makes sense
Delete the Task, as it has the least effect on the score

questions.hint: Reading aloud shows gaps.

questions.prompt: If the form counts characters, what should you check?

options.text: How many names you included
How it counts spaces
How many verbs you used
Whether it counts numbers

questions.hint: The counting rules affect your limit.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is shortest and clearest?

options.text: At that point in time
At the time when this occurred
In due course
Then

questions.hint: 'Then' says the same in one word.

questions.prompt: Why prefer active verbs when cutting?

options.text: They are shorter and show what you did
They hide your role
They are in the future tense
They are more formal

questions.hint: Active verbs are shorter and more direct.

items.title: Level 5: Dealing with a blank mind and nerves at interview
items.body: Nerves are normal, and a blank mind is more common than people expect. It happens when you try to recall a story under pressure. There are practical ways to reduce the risk. First, keep a short note for each story, with five or six trigger words such as a place, a number and an outcome. Look at the notes before you go in. Second, practise telling your stories aloud, so that the words come more easily. Third, breathe slowly and take a moment before you answer. A pause of a few seconds feels long to you but goes unnoticed by the panel. Fourth, if the question seems new, restate it in your own words to give yourself thinking time: 'So you would like an example of working under pressure. One example would be...' Fifth, if your mind goes blank, say so calmly and ask for a moment, or ask to come back to the question later. Sixth, if you realise halfway through that an example does not fit, you may say 'Let me use a different example,' though this is best avoided with preparation. Seventh, if you have misspoken, it is fine to correct a figure or detail briefly. Finally, keep in mind that the panel wants you to do well. They are not trying to catch you out. Arriving early, knowing the route and bringing your documents also reduces stress. Afterwards, you can note what went well and what to improve.

questions.prompt: What is a practical way to avoid a blank mind?

options.text: Skip the notes and rely on remembering things as they come
Keep short notes of trigger words for each story
Memorise a full script for every story in your bank
Avoid practising, so that your answers feel fresh on the day

questions.hint: Trigger words help recall under pressure.

questions.prompt: What do most panels notice about a pause of a few seconds?

options.text: That you are rude
That you are unprepared
Very little
That you should leave

questions.hint: A short pause goes largely unnoticed.

questions.prompt: How can restating a question help?

options.text: It changes the topic
It confuses the panel
It shortens the interview
It gives you thinking time

questions.hint: Restating buys a moment to think.

questions.prompt: If your mind goes blank, what is it acceptable to do?

options.text: Make up something that sounds believable so that you can continue
Walk out of the room to compose yourself for a while
Say so calmly and ask for a moment or to return to it
Change the subject to a topic that you know more about

questions.hint: Honest and calm is fine.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to fix a wrong figure you gave earlier?

options.text: Hope nobody noticed
Correct it briefly
Change the story
Apologise for ten minutes

questions.hint: A brief correction is acceptable.

questions.prompt: How can practising aloud help?

options.text: Words come more easily on the day
It removes nerves entirely
It replaces notes
It shortens the story

questions.hint: Spoken practice builds fluency.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduces stress on the day?

options.text: Skipping breakfast
Arriving early and knowing the route
Arriving at the last minute
Leaving documents at home

questions.hint: Planning ahead reduces stress.

questions.prompt: What attitude do panels usually have?

options.text: They want you to fail
They want to catch you out
They want you to do well
They do not care

questions.hint: Panels are looking for evidence, not trying to trip you.

questions.prompt: If halfway through you realise an example does not fit, what may you do?

options.text: Stop and refuse to answer
Make up an ending
Carry on regardless
Say you will use a different example

questions.hint: Switching is allowed but best avoided through preparation.

questions.prompt: What is a useful thing to do after the interview?

options.text: Note what went well and what to improve
Never think about it again
Delete your notes
Contact the panel about every answer

questions.hint: Reflection improves future performance.

items.title: Level 5: Weighing up which elements to emphasise
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Not every strength of yours will be wanted for every job, so it helps to decide how to emphasise your evidence. Take two applicants for an Administrative Officer role whose advert lists Behaviours, Ability and Experience of working with data. Applicant one has two years of paid clerical work, but no examples of working with the public. Applicant two has no paid job but has run a community group's membership records for three years and dealt with enquiries from members. Both can make a case. Applicant one should lean on her clerical experience for the data requirement, using specifics such as the volume of records she handled and her accuracy rate, and find a Behaviours example outside work to show how she dealt with people, if the advert asks for it. Applicant two should lean on the membership records for the data requirement, describing the system, the number of records and how she kept them accurate, and use her dealings with members for Communicating and Influencing. Neither should be put off by what she lacks. The advert asks for specific things, and the aim is to give evidence for each of them. A common mistake is to spend most of the space on a strong area that the advert does not ask for. For example, if an applicant is proud of a degree-level course but the job needs no Technical element, the space is better used on the listed Behaviours. Match the evidence to the requirement, and tell the truth.

questions.prompt: Which requirement does Applicant two's membership records best match?

options.text: A strength in public speaking
An Ability test result
A Technical qualification
Experience of working with data

questions.hint: Maintaining records is working with data.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour could Applicant two's dealings with members best support?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Delivering at Pace
Communicating and Influencing
Changing and Improving

questions.hint: Dealing with enquiries from members is communicating.

questions.prompt: What should Applicant one do about the missing public-facing example?

options.text: Leave the requirement blank
Find a Behaviours example outside work
Withdraw the application
Claim she has done it

questions.hint: Evidence can come from any area of life.

questions.prompt: What specifics should Applicant one give about her clerical work?

options.text: Her job title and the name of her employer only
Volume of records handled and accuracy
Her salary and the number of hours she worked
The name of her manager and the size of the office

questions.hint: Specifics turn a claim into evidence.

questions.prompt: Which mistake does the passage warn about?

options.text: Writing answers that come in well under the word limit allowed
Spending most of the space on a strong area the advert does not ask for
Giving too many numbers when describing the records you kept
Using the word I too often when describing what was done

questions.hint: Space should be used on listed requirements.

questions.prompt: An applicant is proud of a degree-level course but the job needs no Technical element. How should she use the space?

options.text: On the listed Behaviours
On the course tutor
On describing the course in detail
On her grades

questions.hint: Match the evidence to the requirement.

questions.prompt: Which approach best summarises the passage?

options.text: Say as much as possible about everything you have done
Hide your weaker areas and stress only the strongest ones
Match the evidence to the requirement and tell the truth
Copy the style of a stronger applicant's answers

questions.hint: Fit and honesty are the aim.

questions.prompt: How should neither applicant react to what she lacks?

options.text: Not be put off, and give evidence for each requirement
Ignore the requirement and write about something else instead
Make up the missing part so that every box is filled in
Withdraw from the process, as the gap will count against her

questions.hint: The aim is to evidence each requirement truthfully.

questions.prompt: What detail would strengthen Applicant two's data example?

options.text: Number of records and how she kept them accurate
The date on which the community group was founded
A full list of the names of the members on the register
Her opinion of the community group and how it is run

questions.hint: Scale and accuracy are strong evidence.

questions.prompt: Which element is Applicant one's two years of clerical work mainly evidence for?

options.text: Experience
Ability
Strengths
Technical

questions.hint: It shows what she has done and learned.

items.title: Level 5: Putting it together: a worked AO example
items.body: Here is a complete worked example for the Behaviour Managing a Quality Service, built from a home and community background. Situation: 'For two years I have run the weekly sign-in for a parents' toddler group of about thirty families.' Task: 'The register was often wrong and the church that hosts us needed accurate attendance for its insurance, so I took responsibility for making it reliable.' Action: 'I made a simple printed sheet with each child's name, parent and an emergency contact. I checked it against the previous week's before each session, added new families as they arrived, and corrected spelling with parents at the door. I also locked the completed sheet in the church office after each session and photographed it as a back-up. When I found three children listed twice, I merged the entries and told the group leader.' Result: 'Over the next term there were no errors found at the church's audit, and the leader asked me to train two other volunteers on the system. I learned that a quick check at the start of a session saves a lot of correction later.' Notice what makes it work. It names the Behaviour's key themes: accuracy, procedure, records and care for the users. It uses I throughout. It gives numbers and a time period. It includes an honest detail about a mistake being found and fixed. It ends with a lesson. It is about 190 words, which fits a typical limit. An AO assessor can easily score it against the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which sentence in the worked example is the Task?

options.text: The register was often wrong, so I took responsibility for making it reliable.
I made a simple printed sheet with each child's name and contact.
For two years I have run the weekly sign-in for the toddler group.
There were no errors found at the church's audit the next term.

questions.hint: It says what the writer was responsible for.

questions.prompt: Which detail shows care for procedure?

options.text: Checking the sheet against last week's and locking it in the office
Having a good relationship with parents who came to the sessions
Running a busy toddler group for around thirty families each week
Meeting each family at the door and welcoming them to the group

questions.hint: These steps follow a consistent procedure.

questions.prompt: Which detail shows honesty about a mistake?

options.text: Finding three children listed twice and fixing it
Taking a photograph of the sheet as a back-up copy
The training of two other volunteers on the new system
The result of the church's audit in the following term

questions.hint: It admits a problem and shows the fix.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the Result?

options.text: I corrected the spelling of names with parents at the door each week.
I made a printed sheet that listed each child, parent and contact.
The audit found no errors and I was asked to train two volunteers.
For two years I have run the weekly sign-in at the toddler group.

questions.hint: It states outcomes.

questions.prompt: What lesson does the writer state?

options.text: Churches should buy extra insurance for their regular groups
Toddler groups need more volunteers than they usually have
A quick check at the start of a session saves correction later
Registers are unnecessary if the group has fewer than forty families

questions.hint: It is stated in the Result.

questions.prompt: Why is the example suitable for Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: It centres on accuracy, procedure, records and care for users
It centres on leading a team of people through a time of change
It centres on speed and getting through a large amount of work
It centres on learning a new skill and passing it on

questions.hint: Those are the themes of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes the example credible?

options.text: A long list of the writer's personal virtues and qualities
Numbers, a time period and specific steps
A strong opening claim about the writer's reliability
A mention of a well-known person who knows the group

questions.hint: Specifics make it checkable.

questions.prompt: Why is the training of two volunteers a useful detail?

options.text: It shows others trusted the system, which is evidence of a good Result
It makes the answer run closer to the word limit on the form
It shows that she prefers to share work rather than do it alone
It proves that she now holds a management post in the group

questions.hint: A repeat request or trust is proof of success.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long is the example?

options.text: About 20 words
About 1,000 words
About 600 words
About 190 words

questions.hint: It fits a typical word limit.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour theme would the example show if the writer had only run the register faster?

options.text: Leadership
Managing a Quality Service
Developing Self and Others
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Speed and deadlines, not accuracy, point to pace.
